executive_summary: The defining thread of the day is the intensifying power struggle over who controls the future of artificial intelligence, a battle playing out simultaneously in courtrooms and competitive benchmarks. The conclusion of Musk v. Altman — where Elon Musk's lawsuit against OpenAI failed not on its substantive claims about mission betrayal but on a procedural statute of limitations ruling — underscores that the ideological fight over whether AI development serves humanity or concentrated private interests remains unresolved, even as the legal avenue closes. The trial's final week laid bare two competing narratives: Altman as a self-dealing operator who hijacked a nonprofit, and Musk as an AGI power-seeker using litigation as a competitive weapon, leaving the jury and the public without a definitive moral verdict on Silicon Valley's most consequential institutional rupture. Meanwhile, MIT Technology Review's assessment of Google at I/O 2026 — a clear third-place finisher in foundation models, outgunned by Anthropic and OpenAI in coding — confirms that the spoils of this power struggle are already being distributed, with the Altman-led OpenAI emerging as the dominant force Musk originally sought to challenge. The Economist's newsletter question about the backlash against data centers adds a further dimension: the infrastructure required to sustain this AI race carries real societal costs, making the question of who controls these systems not merely a corporate governance matter but a public interest imperative.

newsletters.title: The Morning: The race to control Congress

items.headline: Map quests
items.blurb: History tells us that the party in power generally loses congressional seats in midterm elections. Yesterday's New York Times/Siena poll showed that Democrats should be in a good position to pick some up. Democrats had an 11-point lead when registered voters were asked which party's candidate they would support for Congress — well ahead of where voters ranked Democrats earlier in this cycle, writes Nate Cohn, our chief political analyst. Currently, Republicans hold narrow majorities in both the House and the Senate. Democrats need to gain three seats in the House and four seats in the Senate to flip control of Congress. And polling is an important bellwether for their chances. But congressional maps can confound voter sentiment and polarize races.

items.headline: The Trump loyalty test
items.blurb: One race to watch closely today is the Republican primary in Kentucky, where Representative Thomas Massie, who has clashed with President Trump, is trying to keep his seat against Ed Gallrein, a challenger backed by the president. Kentucky has an unpredictable political landscape. It's a deep-red state with a Democratic governor. One of its senators is an insider's insider, Mitch McConnell, who is retiring. The other is Rand Paul, an outsider libertarian. Will voters prefer their incumbent — a libertarian-leaning maverick — or vote instead for a MAGA-aligned former Navy SEAL with a huge war chest and no experience in holding office? (Yesterday, in an unusual move, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth traveled to Kentucky to stump for Gallrein.)

items.headline: Just … how, Wemby?
items.blurb: Nothing said about Victor Wembanyama today will qualify as hyperbole. That's how good he was in San Antonio's 122-115 double-overtime win in Oklahoma City, which probably qualifies as one of the best NBA playoff games of the last decade. Wembanyama scored 41 points and grabbed 24 rebounds in the win, which gives the Spurs a 1-0 lead in the Western Conference finals over the defending champs.

items.headline: The Habs, away from home
items.blurb: The barn in Buffalo looked incredible for last night's Game 7 between the Canadiens and Sabres, particularly as the game wore on. Montreal took an early 2-0 lead in the first period, but that melted to a 2-2 tie in the third. The Canadiens advance to the Eastern Conference final for the first time since 2021 and get there via two consecutive Game 7 road wins.

items.headline: The PWHL handled business in regulation — barely
items.blurb: Like their city mates, the Montreal Victoire had a chance to close out a series last night, but this was for a title, and the Victoire were 5:30 away from a clean sweep of the Walter Cup Finals. As if they drew it up in a kid's backyard dream, the Ottawa Charge scored two goals in that final 5:30 to turn a 1-0 deficit into a 2-1 lead. Ottawa saved its season and prevented Montreal from celebrating on its ice. Game 4 is Wednesday in Ottawa.

items.headline: Sorsby sues NCAA
items.blurb: As expected, Texas Tech quarterback Brendan Sorsby sued the NCAA to reinstate his eligibility for the upcoming season while he is under investigation for gambling violations. In his affidavit, Sorsby admitted to betting on Indiana while he was a reserve on the Hoosiers roster, and he is ultimately seeking a quick decision so he can apply to the NFL's supplemental draft in June if his college career is done.

newsletters.title: 🔴 Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?

items.headline: Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?
items.blurb: A year ago I reported on the impact of artificial intelligence on the fight against climate change. On the one hand, data centres used a lot of electricity; on the other, that electricity was mostly renewable, and could be used to develop technologies that helped cut emissions around the world. Overall it felt like cause for cautious optimism, especially if—as we argued in an accompanying leader—AI companies would share more information about the impact of their systems to help consumers make informed decisions. A lot has changed since then. Some shifts were predictable. The amount of electricity the AI industry uses has exploded. The biggest models take more energy to train and run than they did last year, and they are being used by more people to do more things more of the time. Some adjustments were grimly inevitable. Where big tech companies once felt bound by promises they had made in a different political era to cut, or even reverse, their emissions, they now seem happy to switch on new gas turbines to power their growing ambitions, although they still generally insist that the extra energy use is just a temporary measure to compensate for a lack of capacity on the electricity grid. Other changes were more surprising. Last year data-centre impacts felt like a niche topic discussed by people interested in the overlap between AI and climate change. Now they are an increasingly important part of national—and international—politics. In America politicians are proposing regional and national moratoriums on construction, prompting entrepreneurs to wonder whether it might be cheaper to launch computers into space rather than fight through the morass on Earth.

longform.title: Here’s why Elon Musk lost his suit against OpenAI
longform.thesis: Elon Musk lost his lawsuit against OpenAI not on the merits of whether OpenAI violated its nonprofit mission, but because the jury found he waited too long to sue, with his claims barred by statutes of limitations.
longform.context: The verdict concludes a high-profile legal battle in which Musk alleged OpenAI breached its founding contract as a nonprofit by shifting toward a for-profit structure — a dispute that sits at the center of ongoing controversy over OpenAI's corporate transformation and governance.
arguments: The jury's ruling was purely procedural: it determined Musk sued too late, not that OpenAI's conduct was lawful — leaving the core question of whether OpenAI violated its nonprofit mission legally unanswered.

The timeline dispute was central: OpenAI argued signs of its for-profit shift were visible as early as 2017, while Musk claimed he only discovered the change in 2022 — a five-year gap that determined whether his claims fell within the statute of limitations.

The verdict does not close the broader fight over OpenAI's structure, as MIT Technology Review explicitly notes 'the fight over OpenAI's structure may not be over,' suggesting further legal or regulatory challenges remain possible.
longform.significance: The ruling shields OpenAI from liability on a technicality while leaving its nonprofit-to-for-profit conversion unexamined by a jury, which means the legitimacy of that transformation remains legally contested. This matters acutely in 2026 as OpenAI pursues full for-profit restructuring and competitors, regulators, and donors watch for precedent on how AI labs can redefine their founding missions. The case illustrates how procedural law can insulate transformative corporate decisions from substantive accountability.
questions_raised: Since no court has ruled on whether OpenAI actually breached its nonprofit mission, what legal or regulatory avenue — state attorney general action, future litigation, or federal oversight — could force a substantive judgment on the legitimacy of its structural conversion?

If OpenAI's for-profit shift was visible as early as 2017, why did Musk — a co-founder — credibly claim unawareness until 2022, and what does that gap reveal about internal governance and transparency at the organization's founding?

longform.title: Musk v. Altman week 3: now the jury will pick a side
longform.thesis: The third and final week of the Musk v. Altman trial centered on dueling credibility attacks — Altman accused of lying and self-dealing, Musk portrayed as an AGI power-seeker — leaving the jury to adjudicate not just a legal dispute but competing narratives about who controls AI's future.
longform.context: This newsletter dispatch, published May 18, 2026, summarizes MIT Technology Review reporter Michelle Kim's courtroom coverage of the concluding week of Elon Musk's lawsuit against Sam Altman and OpenAI, a three-week trial probing OpenAI's contested conversion from nonprofit to for-profit entity.
arguments: Altman's credibility was directly attacked by Musk's legal team, with accusations of lying and self-dealing, targeting his conduct in OpenAI's governance and the nonprofit conversion process.

Musk was counter-characterized by Altman's defense as a 'power-seeker trying to control artificial general intelligence,' reframing the lawsuit as competitive aggression rather than principled concern for AI safety.

The trial surfaced new internal details about OpenAI's contested nonprofit status and its organizational culture, including the symbolic detail of a 'golden trophy of a donkey's ass awarded to an employee who challenged Musk,' illustrating the power dynamics inside early OpenAI.
longform.significance: The verdict will set a legal and reputational precedent for how nonprofit-to-for-profit conversions in AI are scrutinized, with implications for OpenAI's ongoing restructuring. The trial also functions as a public accountability mechanism for two of the most powerful figures shaping AI development, forcing internal documents and conduct into the public record. The jury's choice between the two narratives — Altman as self-dealer versus Musk as control-seeker — will shape how regulators, investors, and the public assign legitimacy in the AI industry.
questions_raised: Whether the jury's verdict will directly affect OpenAI's ability to complete its for-profit conversion, or whether it will remain a reputational judgment without binding structural consequence.

The article does not resolve what internal documents or testimony, if any, provided dispositive evidence on the nonprofit conversion's legality versus both parties' credibility attacks canceling each other out.

longform.title: What to expect from Google this week
longform.thesis: Google enters I/O 2026 as a clear third-place foundation model competitor, with its coding capabilities badly outgunned by Anthropic and OpenAI, even as it retains a genuine lead in AI for science.
longform.context: Written on the eve of Google I/O 2026, this newsletter dispatch responds to a year-long erosion of Google's AI standing — particularly in coding — that has left even DeepMind engineers reportedly relying on Anthropic's Claude Code instead of Google's own tools.
arguments: Google has fallen to third place in foundation models largely because coding benchmarks now define frontier AI reputation, and its tools are 'so dramatically superior' to Google's that DeepMind engineers reportedly had to be permitted to use Claude Code — an internal admission of competitive failure.

Google's clearest remaining strength is AI for science: as the only frontier AI lab with a Nobel Prize (AlphaFold), it has compounded that advantage with tools like the AI co-scientist — described by a Stanford scientist as an 'oracle' — and AlphaEvolve, making any new scientific announcements at I/O consequential even if they receive less press attention than coding.

Google's health AI ambitions are ambiguous: the public launch of AI-powered Health Coach is framed around fitness and diet rather than medical concerns, raising the question of whether Google is genuinely behind OpenAI's ChatGPT Health or is exercising deliberate caution in a high-stakes domain.

Google faces internal political pressure that complicates its 'veneer of neutrality': 600 employees — many from DeepMind — protested a DoD deal in an open letter, and Google signed it the next day, suggesting executive leadership will override dissent while trying to avoid public controversy at the conference.
longform.significance: This piece maps the competitive realignment in frontier AI at a precise inflection point, showing that coding performance has become the primary proxy for model quality — a framing that directly disadvantages Google despite its scientific strengths. It also surfaces the tension between Google's public image of responsible, Nobel-adjacent AI research and the commercial and military deals driving its actual strategy. The juxtaposition of the I/O conference with the concurrent Musk v. Altman trial underscores how thoroughly legal and political drama now shadows technical announcements.
questions_raised: Can Google close the coding gap at all in the near term, given that even its own engineers preferred competitors' tools as recently as a month before I/O — or has it structurally fallen behind in the capability dimension that currently defines frontier AI?

Is Google's restrained approach to health AI (fitness and diet rather than medical advice) a principled risk-management posture or evidence of a broader product execution gap relative to OpenAI's more aggressive health AI deployment?
